name: Emdash
title: Ninebrains vs Emdash
description: Ninebrains is a fork of Emdash. What it keeps, what it adds (lanes, the Brain job graph, verification gates) and when Emdash itself is the better choice.
summary: Ninebrains’ upstream. Broad agent and issue-tracker support, SSH remotes.
answer: Ninebrains is a fork of Emdash, the open-source desktop app for running coding agents in parallel git worktrees, so it keeps Emdash’s worktrees, diffs, pull requests and integrations. Choose Emdash for its many agent CLIs, issue-tracker hand-off and SSH remotes. Choose Ninebrains for a 2x2 lanes grid, a dependency-aware job graph, checks that block completion, and no telemetry.
note: Emdash’s website now calls the open-source app Emdash Classic. It says Classic still gets fixes, but new development has moved to Emdash 2.0. This page compares the open-source app.

what.text: A desktop app for running AI coding agents in parallel, each task in its own git worktree.

agents.text: Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Amp and more.

isolation.text: A git worktree and branch per agent, locally or on remote machines over SSH.

verification.text: Review diffs, create pull requests and inspect CI checks from one place.

telemetry.text: Optional telemetry sent to PostHog, which you can turn off in Settings or with TELEMETRY_ENABLED=false.

chooseThem.text: You use many agent CLIs: Emdash runs Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Amp and more.
You hand issues to agents from Linear, GitHub, Jira, GitLab and other trackers.
You run agents on remote machines over SSH.

chooseUs: You want four agents visible at once in a 2x2 grid of lanes, across worktrees and tabs.
You want a job graph with dependencies and a planner canvas, dispatched to idle lanes.
You want completion blocked until configured checks pass, and no telemetry endpoint at all.
limits: Lanes support Claude Code and Codex today. Other agents, and SSH remotes, still work in Emdash-style tasks inside Ninebrains.
